clue.text: One's liable to get all steamed up when dinner's wanted in a hurry!

definitions.text: One's liable to get all steamed up when dinner's wanted in a hurry!

parts.words: One's liable to get all steamed up when dinner's wanted in a hurry!
parts.note: reads like a harassed person losing their temper over a late meal, but describes a sealed kitchen pot that cooks fast by building up steam

explanation.surface: A hungry household member gets flustered when the evening meal is needed quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Steamed up' looks like temper; it is literal, the steam that builds inside the sealed pan and cooks food fast.
explanation.definitionFit: A sealed pan that traps steam raises the boiling point, so food cooks quickly when time is short.

definitions.meaning: a small gather or crease in cloth or skin
Kipling's 'Puck of Pook's Hill': a native of Pook's Hill would be one of Puck's kind, Puck with the ending -er as in Londoner

explanation.surface: A crease in the landscape of a Kipling hill.
explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's children's book is 'Puck of Pook's Hill'; the second definition treats the answer as 'Puck-er', someone from that hill, like Londoner.
explanation.definitionFit: A crease or small gather of material, as in puckered lips or a puckered seam, is the first sense.

clue.text: Send out of a hole in the ship

parts.note: the Latin prefix ex- means out of or from
a port is a porthole, an opening in a ship's side

explanation.surface: An order to get something off the vessel through an opening in its hull.
explanation.definitionFit: To export goods is to send them abroad for sale.

definitions.meaning: photographs taken from a film, publicity shots of a movie scene
apparatus that distils spirits, so liquors come from it

explanation.surface: A dismissive cry banishing hazy drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Filmy' looks like 'hazy'; it means 'of a film', the single frames used in publicity. 'Liquors hence' means the things liquors come from.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is photos taken from a movie; the other is distilling equipment that produces spirits like whisky.

parts.note: the prefix re- means again
trenches as a verb means digs ditches

explanation.surface: Someone cutting costs by excavating a second time.
explanation.walkthrough: The charade reads in answer order: 're-' (again) comes before the word for digs, though the clue names them the other way round; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To retrench is to cut back spending, the same as making savings.

clue.text: Tudor was upset, not being given a look in

definitions.text: not being given a look in

indicators.note: upset means overturned or thrown into disorder, so the letters of the two words are jumbled

explanation.surface: A Tudor monarch was put out at being left out of things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' rearranges TUDOR WAS. The definition means facing away rather than looking inward.
explanation.definitionFit: Something turned away from the centre faces the outside rather than looking in.

parts.note: suggests a quarry machine, but names a purple-flowered meadow plant whose first part is the old verb for chipping flints and whose second part is any unwanted growth

explanation.surface: A heavy machine for crushing rock at a quarry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' looks like industrial machinery. To 'knap' is to break flints into shape, and the plant is a common wild flower related to thistles.
explanation.definitionFit: This purple-flowered wild perennial of grassland is related to thistles and cornflowers.

clue.text: Imprudence of growing greens with poles interspersed

indicators.note: interspersed means scattered among, so the polar letters are set into the plant word

parts.note: rashes is Scots for rushes, the green plants of Burns's song 'Green grow the rashes, O'
the poles are north and south, N and S
the second pole, south, S

explanation.surface: Recklessness shown by a gardener mixing poles in among the vegetables.
explanation.walkthrough: The poles go in at different places: N after RASH and S at the end. 'Interspersed' allows them to be scattered among the letters of RASHES.
explanation.definitionFit: Rashness is acting without thinking, the lack of caution that imprudence names.

clue.text: Premi re audience of the Tragedy of Othello?

definitions.text: Premi re audience of the Tragedy of Othello?

parts.words: Premi re audience of the Tragedy of Othello?
parts.note: not a first-night theatre crowd but the people of the island where Shakespeare's play is set, who watched its events first-hand

explanation.surface: Who sat in the stalls at the first performance of Shakespeare's tragedy?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Première' suggests opening night; the play's action takes place in Cyprus, so the islanders saw the tragedy happen.
explanation.definitionFit: Othello's later acts are set in Cyprus, so its inhabitants witnessed the real events.

clue.text: Ermine's going south to join a women's war service

definitions.note: read as the plural, more than one ermine

parts.note: the ATS was the Auxiliary Territorial Service, the women's branch of the British Army in the Second World War

explanation.surface: A stoat in winter coat heads off to enlist in wartime women's service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going' and 'join' are links. The ATS was the British Army's women's service in the Second World War.
explanation.definitionFit: An ermine is a stoat in its white winter coat.

parts.note: Lord Kitchener recruited volunteers who signed up; read instead, a kitchener (cook) baking a Swiss sponge has rolled it

explanation.surface: Someone signed up to a Swiss detachment of Kitchener's army.
explanation.walkthrough: Kitchener was the British war minister whose 1914 posters called for recruits; a 'kitchener' is also a cook, and a Swiss roll is a rolled sponge cake.
explanation.definitionFit: To have signed up, as for military service, is to have put one's name on the roll.

definitions.meaning: the capital and harbour of Australia's Northern Territory
the naturalist Charles, author of 'On the Origin of Species'

explanation.surface: A harbour town named in honour of a man called Charles.
explanation.definitionFit: The Northern Territory capital is a seaport, and the naturalist Charles shares its name, which honours him.

parts.note: suggests lively DJs, but asks whether spirits at a séance tilt the furniture, and names what record spinners operate

explanation.surface: A question about whether lively DJs exist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirited' means moved by ghosts: table-turning was a Victorian séance trick. Disc jockeys use the rotating decks of record players.
explanation.definitionFit: Spiritualists at séances were said to make furniture rotate, and DJs spin records on revolving decks.

indicators.note: into here means turned or made into, so the letters of the two words are reshaped

explanation.surface: Boys who curled up become villains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Curled' looks like the anagram signal but is fodder: SONS CURLED, ten letters, is reshaped 'into' the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A crook is a dishonest person, a villain or rogue.

clue.text: Can come around at four in that case

indicators.note: come around means the able word goes round the others, surrounding them

parts.note: can means is able
taken as written
IV is four in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A tin will turn up around four o'clock in that event.
explanation.walkthrough: ABLE is split as ABL...E around AT + IV. 'In that' is a link; 'case' is the grammatical sense, as in Latin.
explanation.definitionFit: In Latin grammar this is the noun case expressing 'by, with or from'.

clue.text: Heard to ridicule a backsliding of a slipper

indicators.note: heard means the phrase is spoken, giving the sound of the entry

parts.note: mock (ridicule) a sin (a backsliding, a moral lapse)

explanation.surface: Someone is overheard mocking a person who has relapsed into a slip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mock a sin' spoken sounds like the answer; a backsliding is a lapse into sin.
explanation.definitionFit: A soft leather shoe of Native American origin is a kind of slipper.

parts.note: suggests an uncle's friendly approaches, but 'uncle' is slang for a pawnbroker, who lends money against goods

explanation.surface: Kindly approaches from an uncle-like figure.
explanation.walkthrough: A pawnbroker is called 'uncle', so what he gives are loans, which share a word with romantic overtures.
explanation.definitionFit: Loans of money and approaches made to someone are both senses of the word.

clue.text: Wide boys Wooster met in the garden

parts.note: broad means wide
Bertie Wooster, P. G. Wodehouse's comic hero, greets his chums as 'old bean'

explanation.surface: Flashy young chancers that Bertie Wooster encountered among the flower beds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wide boys' is British slang for petty crooks, but 'Wide' gives the first word alone. Bertie Wooster, Wodehouse's comic hero, calls his friends 'old bean'.
explanation.definitionFit: These large-seeded beans are a staple crop of the vegetable plot.

parts.note: an ad is an advertising poster
vert is green in heraldry

explanation.surface: A question whether to turn a poster green.
explanation.walkthrough: Vert is the heraldic word for green. As a verb the answer means to turn attention to, refer to.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to turn one's attention to or refer to something.

clue.text: Keep in a body : officer present

parts.note: CO is a commanding officer
here means present, in attendance

explanation.surface: An officer answers the roll call while keeping his unit together.
explanation.definitionFit: To stick together as one mass or group is to stay united.

definitions.meaning: levy or inflict, as a tax or burden
pass off by deception, foist on someone

explanation.surface: Instructions to put something down and then pass it off.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses mean forcing something unwelcome on another: levying a tax, or foisting a fake.

clue.text: Roger, royal tutor, in role of Dr. Johnson

parts.note: as means in the role of
Samuel Johnson was nicknamed 'the great Cham' (a khan or ruler) of literature

explanation.surface: A royal teacher named Roger plays the part of Dr Johnson.
explanation.walkthrough: Roger Ascham was the Tudor scholar who taught Elizabeth I; Smollett called Dr Johnson 'that great Cham of literature'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tudor scholar Roger was tutor to the young Princess Elizabeth.

parts.note: suggests a guards regiment, but names the mess where commissioned officers of a warship eat, 'guard' hinting at a ward or watch

explanation.surface: Commissioned men of a guards regiment.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'ward' is to guard; on a warship the officers' mess carries that word.
explanation.definitionFit: On a warship it is the mess for commissioned officers, and by extension the officers themselves.

definitions.meaning: a dissenter belongs to a breakaway church, being within a sect
a creature with jointed legs and an external skeleton, such as a beetle or ant

explanation.surface: A dissenting creature with jointed legs.
explanation.walkthrough: Split into two words, the answer means 'within a sect', which is what a Nonconformist (a member of a Protestant church outside the Church of England) is.
explanation.definitionFit: A six-legged creature such as a beetle is an arthropod, and 'in sect' describes a Nonconformist.

parts.note: a Latin phrase meaning 'other I': one's own self, yet another person

explanation.surface: A rhetorical answer insisting it was oneself and nobody else.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin phrase means 'other I', a second self that is also someone else, hence 'who else?'
explanation.definitionFit: A second self or alternative personality is still the same person, yet another.

clue.text: Call on him in Eagle Street

parts.note: an erne is a sea eagle

explanation.surface: Pay a visit to a man living in Eagle Street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Call on' looks like visiting; it means call him by this name. 'In' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A man's first name is what one calls him by.

clue.text: So to speak in the way "A. E." writes

indicators.note: in means the jumble sits inside the two initials

parts.note: the two letters A and E, the pen name of the Irish poet George Russell

indicators.note: the way here means a manner or arrangement, so the letters of the word are set out anew

explanation.surface: Speaking figuratively, in the style the Irish poet AE writes.
explanation.walkthrough: AE was the pen name of the Irish poet George Russell. 'The way' rearranges WRITES as SITWER, which goes 'in' between A and E.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases soften a statement, signalling that words are used loosely or figuratively.
